C.mechanism: C has no interfaces, traits, or type-level associations. Structs only hold primitive values or function pointers without compile-time type computation.
C.why: Maintains direct hardware-mapping philosophy where types do not participate in parameterized abstraction.
C.useWhen: Use void* pointers or explicit type tags for generic data representation in C.
C.price: Loss of type safety and inability to bind related types at compile time.

C++.mechanism: Nested member type aliases (using value_type = T;) within class templates, accessed via typename T::value_type, standardized through traits classes (e.g. std::iterator_traits).
C++.why: Provides type metadata on template parameters without dedicated language-level associated type keywords.
C++.useWhen: When authoring STL-compatible containers, iterators, or allocators exposing dependent types.
C++.price: Requires verbose typename disambiguation in dependent contexts; errors manifest as deep template substitution cascades.

Rust.mechanism: Associated types in traits (trait Iterator { type Item; fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>; }). Establishes a 1:1 functional dependency between trait implementor and output type.
Rust.why: Prevents multiple conflicting implementations of the same trait for one type and eliminates redundant type parameters in signatures (RFC 195).
Rust.useWhen: When an interface has an associated output or dependent type that should be uniquely determined by the implementor (e.g. Iterator, Deref, Add).
Rust.price: Cannot implement the same trait multiple times with different associated types on a single type; requires turbofish/equality bounds in complex bounds.

Zig.mechanism: Comptime functions returning structs containing pub const Item = T; type definitions. Zig lacks formal traits or interface declarations.
Zig.why: Unifies type-level metaprogramming with regular imperative code via comptime execution.
Zig.useWhen: When building generic data structures or allocator wrappers exposing inner types.
Zig.price: No formal interface verification until a member accessing the inner type is evaluated by the compiler.

Java.mechanism: Java interfaces do not support associated types. Generic interfaces must use type parameters (e.g. Iterator<E>). Nested member types are static namespaces.
Java.why: Java generics were designed around type erasure and backward compatibility with raw types, avoiding type-level dependencies.
Java.useWhen: Use generic type parameters (Interface<T>) and wildcard bounds (? extends T) for polymorphic collections.
Java.price: Type parameter clutter in generic class signatures; inability to enforce a single unique output type per implementing class.

C#.mechanism: Interfaces rely on generic type parameters (e.g. IEnumerator<T>). C# does not support associated types or type families in interface declarations.
C#.why: Aligns with CLI runtime reified generics model where generic signatures are distinct metadata tokens.
C#.useWhen: Declare generic interfaces with type parameters for collections and algorithms.
C#.price: Combinatorial proliferation of generic type parameters on complex interdependent interfaces.

Kotlin.mechanism: Kotlin relies strictly on generic type parameters on interfaces (e.g. Iterator<out T>). Associated types are not supported.
Kotlin.why: Maintains full interoperability with JVM bytecode and Java type erasure generics.
Kotlin.useWhen: Use generic interfaces with declaration-site variance (in/out) for collection abstractions.
Kotlin.price: Cannot enforce functional dependencies between types without extra type parameters.

Swift.mechanism: associatedtype declarations within protocols (protocol IteratorProtocol { associatedtype Element; mutating func next() -> Element?; }).
Swift.why: Enables protocol-oriented programming with expressive, concise API design without parameter explosion.
Swift.useWhen: When defining protocols whose conforming types determine specific related types (e.g. Collection, Sequence).
Swift.price: Protocols with associated types cannot be used as simple existential types without any Protocol syntax or opaque return types (some Protocol).

Go.mechanism: Go explicitly rejected associated types during the Go 1.18 generics design. Interfaces define only method sets and type constraint sets.
Go.why: Language designers determined associated types added excessive complexity to the type system and compiler.
Go.useWhen: Pass type parameters explicitly to generic functions and types (e.g. func Map[T, U any](...) []U).
Go.price: Every dependent type must be declared as a separate type parameter, increasing signature verbosity.

Python.mechanism: typing.Protocol uses generic type parameters (Protocol[T]). Associated types are emulated via type annotations on class attributes or generic TypeVars.
Python.why: Preserves Python runtime flexibility and duck typing while allowing static type checkers (mypy/pyright) to verify structural subtyping.
Python.useWhen: Define structural protocols with attribute type annotations for static analysis.
Python.price: Purely static verification; not enforced at runtime without third-party validation libraries.

JavaScript.mechanism: JavaScript has no static type system and therefore no associated types or type-level abstractions.
JavaScript.useWhen: Inspect object properties dynamically at runtime.
JavaScript.price: Absence of compile-time type verification for related data structures.

TypeScript.mechanism: Emulated via indexed access types (T["Item"]) and conditional type inference (T extends Iterator<infer R> ? R : never).
TypeScript.why: Allows modeling complex type associations on top of existing JavaScript object property patterns without new runtime constructs.
TypeScript.useWhen: Extracting element or return types from complex third-party library interfaces.
TypeScript.price: Complex conditional type gymnastics; potential compile-time slowdown on deeply recursive types.

Dart.mechanism: Dart relies on parameterized classes and interfaces (e.g. Iterator<E>). No associated type syntax.
Dart.why: Prioritizes clean, predictable object-oriented type hierarchies for UI framework efficiency.
Dart.useWhen: Use generic type parameters on interfaces.
Dart.price: Cannot enforce 1:1 type relationships without passing type parameters through the hierarchy.

Ruby.mechanism: Dynamic object model without static types; associated types do not exist.
Ruby.why: Duck typing and late message binding make compile-time type associations inapplicable.
Ruby.useWhen: Use duck typing conventions (e.g. objects implementing each and yield).
Ruby.price: No compile-time guarantee of type compatibility between related objects.

PHP.mechanism: PHP interfaces support method parameter and return type declarations, but not associated types or generic type parameters.
PHP.why: Gradual typing model focused on runtime type assertions rather than type-level computation.
PHP.useWhen: Use interface method return types or PHPDoc template tags (@template T).
PHP.price: Lack of native type-level association across interfaces.

Haskell.mechanism: Associated type families (type Item a inside class) provided by GHC TypeFamilies extension (Chakravarty et al. 2005).
Haskell.why: Provides a type-level function indexing into types associated with a class instance, avoiding functional dependency boilerplate.
Haskell.useWhen: When a type class has an associated output type (e.g., container element, graph vertex/edge).
Haskell.price: Type family equation solving increases compile times and can lead to complex type error messages.

OCaml.mechanism: Declared in module signatures (module type S = sig type t ... end) and refined via destructive substitution (with type t = ...).
OCaml.why: Central to ML module system, allowing parameterized components (functors) with abstract associated types.
OCaml.useWhen: Defining module interfaces where implementation types are kept abstract or shared across components.
OCaml.price: Signature duplication and module packing/unpacking overhead if used with first-class modules.

Erlang/Elixir.mechanism: Dynamic actor systems; no static type associations exist in Erlang or Elixir protocols.
Erlang/Elixir.why: Dynamic message passing and runtime pattern matching supersede static type relations.
Erlang/Elixir.useWhen: Rely on data structure conventions and runtime protocol dispatch.
Erlang/Elixir.price: No compile-time check of related type contracts.

Lisp/Clojure.mechanism: Protocols dispatch dynamically on the runtime type of the first argument without associated type declarations.
Lisp/Clojure.useWhen: Implement protocols for custom record types or Java classes.
Lisp/Clojure.price: Runtime dispatch overhead; no compile-time relationship verification.

Smalltalk.mechanism: Pure dynamic object-oriented message passing; no type association mechanism.
Smalltalk.why: Language relies entirely on live object message reflection.
Smalltalk.useWhen: Use polymorphic message contracts across classes.
Smalltalk.price: MessageNotUnderstood exceptions if contract is violated at runtime.

Prolog.mechanism: Logic programming over untyped terms; associated types do not exist.
Prolog.why: Computation is performed via relational unification rather than typed evaluation.
Prolog.useWhen: Represent relations using compound functor terms.
Prolog.price: Runtime failure during unification if term structures do not align.

APL/J.mechanism: Array programming over homogeneous multidimensional arrays without abstract type interfaces.
APL/J.why: Focus is on uniform array transformations rather than type hierarchies.
APL/J.useWhen: Transform arrays using primitive verbs and adverbs.
APL/J.price: No type abstraction boundaries for domain entities.

Forth.mechanism: Untyped stack cells manipulated by direct machine-level words.
Forth.why: Radical minimalism: the programmer manages stack layout directly.
Forth.useWhen: Write words operating on known stack cell contracts.
Forth.price: Stack corruption if stack effects are violated.

SQL.mechanism: Relational tables define concrete column types; SQL schemas do not contain abstract associated types.
SQL.why: Relational algebra operates over tuples of concrete domain values.
SQL.useWhen: Define tables, views, and foreign key relationships.
SQL.price: Cannot abstract over schema representations at the SQL language level.

Ada.mechanism: Formal generic packages and generic formal types (type Item is private;) allow generic units to establish type associations at compile time.
Ada.why: Ensures strict static verification and compile-time contract checking for mission-critical systems.
Ada.useWhen: Instantiate generic packages that bundle related types and operations together.
Ada.price: Requires explicit generic package instantiation before use.

Scala.mechanism: Abstract type members (type T) within traits and classes, supporting path-dependent types (val x: p.T) and upper/lower type bounds.
Scala.why: Unifies object-oriented encapsulation with module-level type abstraction and path-dependent typing.
Scala.useWhen: When designing polymorphic components with dependent types where type parameter syntax is too verbose.
Scala.price: Complex type system interactions; path-dependent typing rules increase compiler complexity.
